active_trends.text: US removal of climate from security *vehicles*, not just language. The inverse operation identified last week is now the dominant one and it has multilateral cover: the security vocabulary retained with the climate referent removed, written into the G20 Critical Minerals Meeting Communiqué under the formula 'different domestic pathways'.

US adaptation surviving only where reframed as disaster operations. Extended this week by the level rather than the register: the climate-security institute's most regular product is now a state-level briefer on installations, infrastructure and local economies, which is the disaster-operations frame with a statehouse reader.
UNSC shift from "climate security" to "natural resource governance". September's programme of work under the French presidency contains neither; the month's substantive debate is peacekeeping reform.

Retreat from binding multilateral environmental instruments. Per the 2026-09-06 pushback, do not extend this trend to cover institutional candour about overshoot; the two are different acts and merging them makes the trend unfalsifiable. The voluntary-cooperation language in this week's G20 communiqué belongs here rather than under securitisation.

Dutch institutional creation with fiscal non-commitment. Last week's counter-instance has been reversed: the deltacommissaris named the money before the budget, and the budget funded flood defence while reducing longer-term provision for the two priorities the review called underfunded. The defence side still fits — climate is mission-critical in the budget's own words, with €5m structural and no action plan two and a half months on.

Dutch public-opinion decline against the international average. Refreshed this week for the first time in four, against the Netherlands Institute for Social Research's *Klimaat en samenleving 2026* of 27 May 2026: 34 per cent angry about the attention climate receives against other social problems, up from 24 per cent in 2025, with costs widely seen as unfairly split between citizens and companies. The trend stands; its evidence is four months old rather than unverified.

Overshoot moving from a risk to a planning premise. Still no security institution using the term. Note a nearby development that is not the same thing: 'beyond adaptation limits' is now in circulation as an attribution finding, which is a claim about a specific event rather than about a global trajectory. Do not merge them.

High-mountain hazard migrating from the glacial-lake-outburst mode monitoring was built for to ice-and-rock slope failure it was not, across borders where no data-sharing mechanism exists. Strengthened decisively this week: the attribution study concludes that no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time for this event, which converts the mismatch from an institutional criticism into a published scientific finding. The border half is unmoved — China's commitment to work towards a hydrological agreement produced nothing datable.

The gap between what event attribution will certify and what climate finance is asked to pay for. Substantially revised this week and the framing was wrong: attribution did not certify the event and did not refuse the case. It attributed the hazard environment, declined the event counterfactual, and grounded the policy conclusion in adaptation limits instead. The live question is no longer whether the methods or the standard of evidence gives first, but whether an adaptation-limits argument is adjudicable by the institutions that will now receive it.

Climate argued in whichever security register is locally unoccupied — economic security in Europe, energy security in the US — rather than in the field's own. Two additions this week, in opposite directions: the substitution reached a negotiated multilateral text at the G20, and the adaptation-finance community reached for human security and global stability to argue a financing case. Both are substitutions and a field that scores only one as a loss is measuring nothing.

The assets a changing hazard environment destroys are increasingly ones that are publicly indispensable and privately owned, which leaves no instrument settling who pays. Nepal's flood put roughly seventy per cent of about Rs408 billion in losses on the private sector, with damaged hydropower and solar generation of 759 MW the largest single line and eight of thirteen hydropower projects privately held — the same asset class a paper read in this digest last week identified as the route by which climate investment brings security forces into mountain life. Vital enough to be guarded, private enough that the loss is not the state's.

open_threads.text: PSI's current funding phase. Unchanged and the re-check is weaker for a second week: clingendael.org refused retrieval again, so this rests on search. The only publicly datable phase announcement remains the institute's of 9 December 2019, with no renewal announced in nearly seven years. The role-description discrepancy on van Schaik is carried alongside it and cannot be resolved while the institute's pages are unreachable.

Whether NATO published a 4th Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment. Re-checked against NATO's own topic page for a third consecutive week: the series is listed for 2022, 2023 and 2024 and nothing since, and the most recent item of any kind on the page is from June 2025. Two annual cycles missed with no announcement. The thread stays open because what is missing is not the document but any NATO statement about it.

Whether the IMCCS World Climate and Security Report has formally lapsed. Re-checked against imccs.org: no report since the 2024 edition and the most recent item of any kind remains the open letter of 23 October 2025. One thing was resolved on the side: the council's chair is confirmed on its own site as General Tom Middendorp, retired Chief of Defence of the Netherlands, and Erin Sikorsky is confirmed as its director.

CSM funding trajectory. Not advanced; no output in the window and the annual financial report was not retrieved. Structure documented through 2028, volumes not, and the volumes are the part that would show a trajectory.

MFF 2028-2034 climate/security line. Not advanced for a second week. The European Parliament Think Tank study ECTI_STU(2026)780419 on the climate and environmental impacts of the budget proposals still exists in the catalogue and its page still returns no content. It remains the most likely single source for whether a security-tagged climate earmark exists, and the thread cannot move without it. Try a different route next week — the committee's own document register rather than the Think Tank catalogue.

Chinese 2026 defence doctrine on climate — gap. Re-checked; unchanged in its fifth week. The negative observable has sharpened: China stated in early September that it would work with Nepal towards signing a transboundary hydrological information agreement and establish a regular cooperation mechanism, and nothing datable happened on it between 14 and 20 September — in the week the attribution science on the shared hazard was published and while China shares data year-round with five Mekong states.

Any Indian security document on climate — gap. Re-checked; unchanged. India carried its climate record into a G20 energy ministerial with no climate pillar and received a climate-justice reconstruction claim from Nepal, answering it procedurally. Neither produced a doctrinal text.
Swiss Re sigma citation for the $424bn 2025 protection gap.
open_threads.resolution: The citation is **sigma 1/2026**, *Natural catastrophes in 2025: the persistent rise of wildfire and storm risk*, Swiss Re Institute. The protection gap of $424 billion for 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024, with the natural catastrophe resilience index broadly stable at 27.3 per cent, comes from the Institute's Natural Catastrophe Insurance Resilience Index and is expressed in premium-equivalent terms. Caveat on strength: the reinsurer's own page would not open and the mirrored PDF's text could not be extracted, so the figures are corroborated across Swiss Re's own social post and several independent trade reports rather than read off the document.

open_threads.text: Whether any event attribution study of the 26 August Langtang-Lirung cascade appears.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved on 17 September 2026, and the answer is not one of the two the thread was framed to expect. World Weather Attribution published *Rapid Warming in the Himalaya Exacerbates Geohazard Cascades Beyond Adaptation Limits*, with contributors in ten countries across glaciology, mountain hydrology, climate science, seismology, humanitarian practice and social science. It attributes the hazard environment and not the event: about 1.5°C added to July-August temperatures by human-caused climate change, about 2°C annually — larger than global mean warming — individual winter months as much as 3°C, and the 0°C isotherm rising roughly 100 metres a decade into the bedrock that failed. It states explicitly that it has not assessed whether this specific rock-ice avalanche would have occurred without human-induced climate change, while asserting that warming at a rate beyond the global mean increases the likelihood and severity of such hazards. It then concludes that the event exceeded the design and predictive limits of existing risk reduction, that no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time, that this constitutes a soft limit to adaptation given constrained habitable land and population increase, and that addressing loss and damage through recovery and reconstruction has become an unavoidable part of climate response. So: no event attribution, a hazard-environment attribution, and the policy conclusion reached through adaptation limits instead of causation. The successor question is the `adaptation-limits-adjudication` thread. Reporting figures that travelled with it: the debris flood ran 200 km in under seven hours at average speeds around 188 km/h and deposited 30.5 million cubic metres of material.

open_threads.text: What the HiRISK consortium is: membership, funding, institutional home.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved from hirisk.org, which was opened and read. HiRISK describes itself as 'a loose consortium of experts from High Mountain Asia and beyond', producing open risk datasets, dashboards, an expert database, risk assessments and peer-reviewed papers. Its listed member organisations include the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, the University of Central Asia in Tajikistan, a research group in Pakistan, a mountain-hazards institute in China, a hydrological institute in Bhutan, and two regional agencies including the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat. Stated support comes from Geo Mountains and from the Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains standing group of the International Association of Cryospheric Sciences and the International Permafrost Association. Funding amounts and sources are not disclosed, no individuals are named, and the site is labelled beta. Cite it as a consortium finding attributed to the consortium; do not upgrade it to institutional authority.

open_threads.text: What standard of evidence the Loss and Damage Fund applies to a claim from an event with no event-level attribution. Advanced and complicated this week. The attribution finding that arrived is not the causal certificate the question assumed; it is an adaptation-limits finding, which speaks more directly to the fund's own premise than a causal attribution would. Meanwhile the fund's practice is running ahead of its doctrine in a way this digest missed: $20 million was allocated to Nepal on 9 September under the Barbados Implementation Modalities on proposals predating the flood, and the co-chairs replied to the emergency request of 31 August on 10 September without committing anything. With no extraordinary meeting convened and the tenth board meeting expected before 10 December in Manila, the standard looks likely to be set by what the board does with a specific request on a specific date rather than by any stated principle.

Whether any part of the deltacommissaris's ask — 1 per cent of GDP to at least 2 — survives into a government commitment, and whether the review's concession that some damage will not be prevented is adopted in cabinet language or quietly dropped. First checkpoint passed and the answer is partial and negative: the Prinsjesdag budget of 15 September funded water safety while, on the province of Groningen's reading of 16 September, reducing longer-term provision for climate adaptation, freshwater availability and integrated water policy — the two priorities the review named as underfunded. Nothing opened engages the 2-per-cent figure. The cabinet's formal response to the Deltaprogramma 2027, which normally follows within days of Prinsjesdag, is the next and more direct checkpoint. Still open, and now with a specific question attached: whether the concession about unpreventable damage appears in cabinet language at all.

Whether an adaptation-limits argument is adjudicable by the institutions that will now receive it. The attribution network has relocated the evidentiary basis of a loss and damage claim from 'did warming cause this' to 'was this beyond what adaptation could have prevented'. The second question has a literature and a vocabulary — hard and soft limits, constraints, maladaptation — and no institutional procedure. A fund board, a development bank or a court asked to apply it has no threshold, no method and no precedent, where a causal attribution at least came with a probability. Watch for the first body that tries: the terms it reaches for will become the standard by default, exactly as this digest predicted would happen with causation.

Who bears roughly Rs300 billion of privately held losses in Nepal, and whether a sovereign loss and damage claim can cover them. The Rapid Disaster Needs Assessment puts about seventy per cent of about Rs408 billion in damage on the private sector, with 759 MW of damaged hydropower and solar — eight of thirteen hydropower projects privately owned — the largest single line at about Rs151 billion. A claim on a multilateral fund is a claim for public reconstruction; these are private balance sheets. Either the state recovers on behalf of private owners, which is a fiscal transfer nobody has argued for in public, or the headline reconstruction figure and the claim are measuring different things. No insurance recovery figure has been published, which is the number that would say whether this is a solvency problem for Nepali generators or a claims event for global reinsurance. The fuller needs assessment, due around mid-October, has to address it.

open_moves.text: Denmark's UNSC food-security debate, outcome document unconfirmed. Unchanged; September's Council programme of work under the French presidency carries no food-security item and the month's substantive debate is peacekeeping reform.

CSR/CCS philanthropic-funding bet. Advanced on activity and leadership, not on money. The institute published twice in this window (B6, D5) and its own pages confirm Erin Sikorsky as director of both the Center and the International Military Council on Climate and Security, with Tom Ellison as deputy director and John Conger as director emeritus, alongside four named fellows and roughly twenty-five non-resident fellows. Staffing looks intact and funding remains undocumented. The more interesting question has shifted from whether the institute survives to whom it is now writing for.

NUPI/SIPRI Abyei report and the next UNISFA renewal. The report half is answered: *Beyond the Blue Line: Tackling Climate, Peace, and Security Challenges in Abyei*, by Katongo Seyuba of SIPRI's climate change and risk programme and Andrew E. Yaw Tchie of the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs, published by SIPRI in Stockholm in August 2026, on how changing rainfall, extreme heat, flooding and drought affect livelihoods and local conflict dynamics and constrain the UN force's mobility and access. Open on the mandate renewal, which is where the report's recommendations would or would not appear.

EU integrated framework for climate resilience. Re-checked: still 'expected to be adopted during the second half of 2026', no draft published, no slippage announced. Third-party analysis describes the Water Resilience Strategy as due by the end of 2026 and as dependent on alignment with this framework, which makes the framework's timing the constraint on both. The standing date correction holds: the call for evidence closed 4 September **2025**, not 2026.

UNSG succession, finalisation Aug-Oct 2026. Nothing datable in this window. Straw polls were held 30 July and 21 August, with Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett leading the second on eight 'encourage' votes and Rebeca Grynspan and Rafael Grossi on seven each; further rounds were expected in September under the French presidency but not during high-level week, which begins after this window closes. Guterres's term ends 31 December 2026. Still nothing found on what any candidate has said about Council competence over climate, which remains the highest-value unanswered question here.

COP31 Antalya, 9-20 November 2026. The presidency's credibility is now being contested in public, on fossil-fuel expansion rather than on security: an argument published 18 September records Türkiye at 56 per cent of electricity from coal and gas in 2025 with wind and solar at 22 per cent, and Australia above 60 per cent fossil with coal at 45 per cent and the world's third-largest fossil-fuel export position, neither with binding phase-out timelines. No part of the argument is being made in the security register by anyone.

Whether 'overshoot' is adopted as a planning premise by security institutions or stays inside the climate-policy system. No movement. Guard against a false positive: 'beyond adaptation limits' entered circulation this week as an attribution finding about one event, which is not the same claim as overshoot as a planning premise, and counting it as the tell firing would make this thread unfalsifiable.

Whether AOSIS's legal-character defence of 1.5°C holds through UNGA81 and COP31. No AOSIS statement in the window. Its chair remains Ilana Victorya Seid, Permanent Representative of Palau to the UN. Adjacent and worth reading before the next digest: the Pacific Islands Forum leaders' meeting in Palau in early September adopted a declaration on urgent and inclusive climate action to keep 1.5°C within reach, which this digest has not yet read.

Whether the pre-event-indications finding produces a funded glacier-hazard early-warning programme, and whether it can survive the China-Nepal data-sharing wall. Complicated rather than advanced. The attribution study concludes that no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time for this event, which cuts against the premise that better warning was the missing piece — and strengthens the case for a programme aimed at slope monitoring rather than lake monitoring. No funded programme appeared, and no data-sharing agreement was signed.

Whether Nepal's restriction of foreign search-and-rescue becomes a precedent or an episode. The file has turned further outward: Nepal's active demand is now reconstruction finance across bilateral and multilateral venues (D4), on top of the inward demand for real-time Chinese hydrological data. Still open on whether any transboundary early-warning mechanism emerges; China's stated intention to work towards an agreement produced nothing datable this week.

Whether the UNFCCC secretariat's economic-security framing is picked up outside the climate-policy system, and in particular whether any EU security institution adopts the formulation. No movement: nothing from the European External Action Service, the Commission's defence side or a member-state ministry in this window. One week is not an answer, and the high-level week that follows this window is the better test.

Whether the deltacommissaris's two-per-cent-of-GDP ask converts into any government commitment. First checkpoint passed with a partial negative (B2, D3): the budget funded water safety and, on a provincial government's reading, reduced longer-term provision for the two priorities the review named as underfunded, with nothing opened engaging the figure itself. The cabinet's formal response to the Deltaprogramma 2027 is the next checkpoint and normally arrives within days of Prinsjesdag.

Whether Nepal's reconstruction bill produces a Loss and Damage Fund response, and on what evidentiary basis. Advanced on both halves. The fund has already allocated $20 million under the Barbados Implementation Modalities, reported 9 September, on proposals predating the flood — so the first disbursement to the claimant is not a response to the disaster at all. The emergency request of 31 August has been acknowledged by the co-chairs and not scheduled. And the evidentiary basis has changed shape: what is now available is an adaptation-limits finding rather than a causal attribution. The grants-versus-loans question moved too and not in Nepal's favour: every venue on the finance minister's October itinerary is a lender.
Whether the rescission was announced as expected, whether the endangerment-finding proposal followed, and whether the Houston ministerial's outcome document mentions climate.
open_moves.resolution: All three answered. The partial repeal of the carbon pollution standards for fossil-fuel-fired power plants was finalised on 14 September 2026 by Administrator Lee Zeldin, signed at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston rather than on its sidelines; the agency prices it at $310 billion in savings and calls it the largest power-sector deregulatory action in US history. The separate proposal followed simultaneously: EPA proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse-gas standard for the sector, the vehicle for repealing the power-plant endangerment finding, with $370 million in claimed direct compliance-cost savings. And the ministerial's outcome document, a Critical Minerals Meeting Communiqué, does not mention climate: it grounds critical minerals in energy security, digital infrastructure, emerging technologies and economic development, and calls for voluntary and collaborative cooperation respecting national sovereignty and 'different domestic pathways'. Canada's own readout of the meeting likewise contains no reference to climate change. Environmental organisations have said they will litigate. The substitution this digest read off the ministerial's branding last week is confirmed in a negotiated multilateral text, which is why this closes as landed rather than as too early.

open_moves.text: Whether NATO ever states what happened to the Secretary-General's annual Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment, now two cycles missed without announcement, and whether the STO's SAS-182 route becomes the permanent home of the analytical work. Re-checked against NATO's own topic page for a third week: nothing. Continued silence is itself the finding and should be re-recorded each week rather than assumed. A statement either way would close this.

Whether the relocation of the evidentiary question from causation to adaptation limits is taken up by the institutions that have to apply it — a fund board, a development bank, a court, a security institution — or stays a finding in a research product. Two things would confirm it: a loss and damage decision reasoning from adaptation limits rather than attribution, and any security institution using the argument that a hazard class has outrun early warning. Two things would refute it: the finding being cited publicly as an event attribution, which is already beginning, or the adaptation-limits language being absorbed into the general adaptation-finance ask, which would make it a fundraising phrase rather than an evidentiary standard.

Whether the American climate-security field's move to the state level is a durable relocation or a holding pattern. The measurements are specific: whether the state briefer series continues at pace and adds states with large installations, whether any state government is named as a commissioner or partner, and whether the institute's international and doctrinal output recovers if federal space reopens. Watch also for the same move by others — a second US institute writing for statehouses would make this a field-level shift rather than one organisation's strategy.

Whether the asymmetry in the Dutch budget — flood defence funded, spatial adaptation and freshwater reduced over the longer term — survives the cabinet's formal response to the Deltaprogramma 2027 and the autumn budget debates, or is corrected by amendment. The underlying question is more general than the Dutch case and is why this is tracked as a move rather than a line item: whether a government that has accepted in principle that some climate damage cannot be prevented will fund the diffuse, unprocurable half of adaptation, or only the half that can be built by contractors against a statutory norm.
